newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australia November current account data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australia November current account data.

text.p: Australia's seasonally adjusted current account deficit came in at A$1.923 billon in November, compared with median forecasts for a A$1.75 billion deficit.
Estimates for November had ranged from A$1.5 to A$1.9 billion after the A$1.8 billion short fall in October.
Also released were ANZ's monthly jobs advertisements series for December, which fell 3.9 percent.
The following is a selection of economists' initial reation to the data.
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA

"Clearly the result was larger than we, and the market, were expecting. Exports are the wild card always in these numbers month to month and disappointingly weak. We were expecting a small uptick and they have actually fallen five percent, and I think that largely accounts for the higher-than-expected deficit this month."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK

"Obviously, it was little bit higher than expected, but it mainly seems to be because of a deterioration on the trade side. I think bascially what we're seeing is the income deficit putting a floor under the current account of about A$1.7 billion a month, and basically we're just going to see fluctuations around that level depending on what happens with the trade deficit each month."
SUSAN CREIGHTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST ABN AMRO:

"It is a concern that exports were down by that five percent in the month, it's a lot weaker than what we were looking (for). Certainly into 1997 we do expect that moderately stronger growth in Australia's major trading partners should be a support for our export markets, but on the other hand we do expect that there will be upward pressure on imports on the back of stronger business investment through 1997. So really, the outlook for the current account deficit is with upward pressure,...and you're going to continue to get monthly current account deficit readings of between A$1.7 and A$2.0 billion.
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST CITIBANK AUSTRALIA

"There must be some sort of hint of concern for the authorities with the current starting to deteriorate. The trend is certainly moving wider at a time when the economy is pretty soft. If we do get these investment numbers realised and consumers start spending a little bit of money, we get a big rise in imports and the current account blows out again. It's a little premature to say that at the moment, but precursors for some current account widening after starting to fliter through already."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP

"Overall it's a disappointing number but the current account does not contain major implications for monetary policy and I would not expect this number to have a major impact on the thinking of the Reserve Bank." He said the income deficit figure for November was an extrapolation only and the real number could force a revision of the current account deficit to above A$2 billion for November. "That said, I don't think we will see seriously worse figures than this over the first few months of 1997 and that's partly because I think the economy is remaining fairly flat."
